\section[niger, albus]{niger, albus — Latin's black and white, each with a shine-twin}

\label{lesson:LA-C06-niger-albus}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've seen \textbf{niger} already, hiding inside French \emph{noir} and Spanish \emph{negro}. Here's what those daughter languages left behind: Latin didn't have just one word for black, or just one for white — it had \textbf{two of each}, split by \textbf{brightness}, not just hue.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Two blacks, two whites}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{niger} = "black" with a \textbf{gleam} — a shiny, lustrous black. This is the one that survives into Romance (\emph{noir, negro, nero}).
  \item \textbf{āter} = "black" that's \textbf{dull, matte, lightless} — the flatter, duller black. (English keeps a fossil of it in \textbf{atrocious} and \textbf{atrocity} — something so dark/dreadful it's "black" in the \emph{āter} sense.)
  \item \textbf{albus} = "white" that's \textbf{plain, dull, matte} — this is the one that mostly faded from Romance's everyday vocabulary (surviving in Spanish \emph{alba}/French \emph{aube}, "dawn," rather than as the everyday color word).
  \item \textbf{candidus} = "white" with a \textbf{shine, a gleam, a glow} — bright white. English keeps this one working hard: \textbf{candid} (originally "shining bright," then "morally bright/honest"), \textbf{candidate} (Romans running for office wore a bleached, gleaming-white toga, the \emph{toga candida}), and \textbf{candle}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Romance languages mostly \textbf{dropped} this shine-vs-matte split and kept only one word per color (\emph{niger} survived for black; \emph{albus} and \emph{candidus} both survive, but neither became the plain everyday "white" in most daughter languages — Spanish and French instead borrowed a \textbf{Germanic} word, \emph{blanco/ blanc}, for their everyday white, as you may already have seen). So Latin's four color-words shrank to cover just two basic ideas — brightness stopped being how Latin-descended languages sort black and white.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "niger" — gleaming black — then "āter," dull black{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "albus" — dull white — then "candidus," shining white{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the English fossils — "atrocious" (āter), "candid, candidate" (candidus){]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What distinguished Latin's two black words, and its two white words? (\textbf{Brightness} — \emph{niger} "gleaming black" vs. \emph{āter} "dull black"; \emph{candidus} "shining white" vs. \emph{albus} "dull white.") Which two English words come from \emph{candidus}, and why does \emph{candidate} mean what it does? (\textbf{Candid} and \textbf{candidate} — Roman office-seekers wore a bleached-white \emph{toga candida}.) Did Romance keep this four-way split? (\textbf{No} — it settled on one plain word per color, and Spanish/French even borrowed a \textbf{Germanic} word for everyday white.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ruber, caeruleus]{ruber, caeruleus — a rock-solid red, and a shaky blue}

\label{lesson:LA-C06-ruber-caeruleus}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} One of these two words is about as old and stable a color-word as language gets. The other is a genuine puzzle — because Latin, like a surprising number of ancient languages, never quite settled on a clean word for "blue."
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ruber} ("red") descends from PIE \emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-}}, a root so old it also gives English \textbf{red}, \textbf{rust}, \textbf{ruddy}, and German \textbf{rot}. Latin's own family used \textbf{two} everyday variants of this root — \textbf{rubeus} and \textbf{russus} — and Romance split them between languages: French \textbf{rouge} comes from \emph{rubeus}; Spanish \textbf{rojo} comes from \emph{russus}. Different Latin words, same ancient root, same color.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
You might expect a clean Latin ancestor for "blue" the way \emph{ruber} is for red. There isn't really one. \textbf{Caeruleus} is the closest word Latin had — and it's a much fuzzier idea than \emph{ruber}: it covers the color of the \textbf{sky} and the \textbf{sea} (\emph{caeruleum mare}, "the blue/dark sea"), but it can also shade toward \textbf{dark green} or simply "\textbf{dark}," depending on context. It isn't a fixed, single hue-word the way \emph{ruber} clearly is.

This isn't just a Latin quirk. Classicists and linguists have long noted that \textbf{many ancient languages lacked a clean, stable basic word for blue} — Ancient Greek is the most famous case (Homer's "\textbf{wine-dark sea}," never a simple "blue sea"). Across many language families, "blue" tends to be one of the \textbf{last} basic color words to settle into place, historically — sometimes splitting off late from words that also covered green, dark, or grey. Latin's \emph{caeruleus} looks like part of that same broader pattern, though the exact reasons are still debated among linguists rather than fully settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ruber" — red — the ancient, PIE-rooted color word{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: its two children — "rubeus $\to$ French rouge," "russus $\to$ Spanish rojo"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "caeruleus" — sea/sky-colored — Latin's shakiest, least fixed color word{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What PIE root gives \textbf{ruber}, and what English words share it? (\emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-}} — \textbf{red, rust, ruddy}.) Which two Latin red-words split between French and Spanish, and which went where? (\textbf{Rubeus $\to$ French rouge}; \textbf{russus $\to$ Spanish rojo}.) Why is \textbf{caeruleus} a shakier word than \emph{ruber}? (\textbf{It covers sea/sky and can shade toward dark or green} — it was never a single fixed "blue," a pattern linguists have noticed across many ancient languages, most famously Greek's "wine-dark sea.")
\end{tcolorbox}
